summary: Defines MIB objects for managing RS-232-like hardware devices using SMIv2. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP is a way for a network manager to read and set values on a device. This RFC defines the values that describe a serial port: its speed, its character settings, its error counters and the state of the modem control signals.

questions: which snmp objects manage serial ports
how do i read modem signals with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for reading and setting serial ports: speeds, framing, error counts and modem signals.

tldr.problem: Network devices have serial ports, such as RS-232, and managers had no standard SNMP objects for their speed, character settings, error counts or modem control signals.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module, rs232, placed at transmission 33. It has one base object, a general port table, separate tables for asynchronous and synchronous ports, and input and output control signal tables, plus conformance groups.
tldr.outcome: It is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1317. It models the physical layer, so higher-layer MIBs such as the Character MIB sit on top of it.

facts.value: one base object and four tables

facts.value: other, rs232, rs422, rs423, v35, x21

today: RFC 1659 is a Draft Standard published in July 1994. It obsoletes RFC 1317, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1659 defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing RS-232-like hardware devices. It was produced by the IETF Character MIB Working Group and obsoletes RFC 1317.

The MIB applies to interface ports that might logically support the Interface MIB, a Transmission MIB, or the Character MIB. The most common example is an RS-232 port with modem signals. The RS-232-like Hardware Port MIB includes RS-232, RS-422, RS-423, V.35, and other asynchronous or synchronous serial physical links with a similar set of control signals.

Because the MIB covers several similar kinds of hardware, it contains objects that do not apply to all of them. The compliance definitions therefore have a general group for all implementations, and separate groups for the different types of ports, such as asynchronous and synchronous. The MIB is mandatory for all systems that have such a hardware port supporting services managed through some other MIB.

The objects relate to physical layer connections. Such connections may provide hardware signals other than those for basic data transfer, such as RNG and DCD, and hardware ports also have attributes such as speed and bits per character.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP gives a manager a standard way to read and set numbers on a device. This RFC lists the numbers that describe a serial port: how fast it runs, how many bits each character uses, how many characters were damaged, and whether each control wire is on or off. Any device with such a port must publish these numbers.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Framework Behind It
sections.content:
The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework consists of four major components. RFC 1442 defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. STD 17, RFC 1213, defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols. RFC 1445 covers the administrative and other architectural aspects of the framework. RFC 1448 is the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base or MIB. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) defined by the SMI. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name, and the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. For human convenience a textual string, termed the descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type.
sections.plainLanguage: Every value in an SNMP MIB has a unique name, like an entry in a phone book, and a manager reads or writes it by that name. This RFC's names all sit under one module called rs232, placed at transmission 33.

sections.title: Layering and the Interface MIB
sections.content:
The RS-232-like MIB is one of many MIBs designed for layered use, as described in the Interface MIB (RFC 1573). In most implementations where it is present it will be in the lowest interface sublayer. The RS-232-like MIB represents the physical layer, providing service to higher layers such as the Character MIB (RFC 1658) or the PPP MIB (RFC 1471).

The Interface MIB's ifTestTable and ifRcvAddressTable are not relevant to the RS-232-like MIB. The RS-232-like MIB is relevant for the ifType values rs232(33) and v35(45), and perhaps others. It requires the conformance groups ifGeneralGroup and ifFixedLengthGroup.

The RFC also states two relationships to the Interface MIB. The value of ifSpeed is the same as rs232PortOutSpeed, and the usefulness of the error counters in this MIB depends on the octet counters in ifFixedLengthGroup.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB describes the physical layer, the wires themselves, and other MIBs describe the layers above. A manager therefore uses this MIB for the port itself and a separate MIB for the character stream or the point-to-point link control that runs over it.

sections.title: The Tables
sections.content:
The module comprises one base object and four tables. The base object, rs232Number, gives the number of ports, regardless of their current state, in the general port table.

The rs232PortTable holds a row for every port. Each row has an index, the port type (other, rs232, rs422, rs423, v35 or x21), the number of input and output signals, the input and output speeds in bits per second, and the input and output flow control type. The index is an InterfaceIndex, the same value as ifIndex. The RFC notes that, by convention and if possible, hardware port numbers map directly to external connectors, and that the value for each port must remain constant at least from one re-initialization of the network management agent to the next.

The rs232AsyncPortTable holds settings and error counters for asynchronous ports, and its entries need not exist for synchronous ports. The rs232SyncPortTable does the same for synchronous ports. The rs232InSigTable and rs232OutSigTable hold one row per port and signal for the input and output control signals.

The signal tables contain entries only for signals that the software can detect, for inputs, or can assert, for outputs, and that are useful to observe.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has one count object and four tables. The general table has a row for every port. The asynchronous and synchronous tables hold extra settings for the two kinds of port. The two signal tables have one row for each control wire that the software can read or drive.

sections.title: Port Settings and Error Counters
sections.content:
In the general table, rs232PortInSpeed and rs232PortOutSpeed are read-write and give the port's speed in bits per second. The RFC notes that non-standard values, such as 9612, are probably not allowed on most implementations. The flow control types are none, meaning no flow control at this level, ctsRts and dsrDtr, meaning use of the indicated hardware signals.

For asynchronous ports, the writable settings are rs232AsyncPortBits, the number of bits in a character, with the range 5 to 8; rs232AsyncPortStopBits, with the values one, two, oneAndHalf and dynamic; rs232AsyncPortParity, with the values none, odd, even, mark and space; and rs232AsyncPortAutobaud, which is enabled or disabled and controls the port's ability to sense the input speed automatically. When autobaud is enabled a port may autobaud to values different from the set values for speed, parity and character size, so a management system may temporarily observe values different from what it previously set.

Three counters tally problems on asynchronous ports. rs232AsyncPortParityErrs counts characters with a parity error, rs232AsyncPortFramingErrs counts characters with a framing error, and rs232AsyncPortOverrunErrs counts characters with an overrun error. Each counts from system re-initialization and while the port state was up or test.

For synchronous ports, rs232SyncPortClockSource gives the source of the port's bit rate clock: internal, external, or split, which means the transmit clock is internal and the receive clock is external. The synchronous counters cover frames with an invalid frame check sequence, frames that failed to be transmitted because data was not available to the transmitter in time, frames that failed to be received because the receiver did not accept the data in time, frames interrupted by loss of modem signals, and frames aborted by an abort sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: Some settings are read-write, so a manager can change them: the speed in bits per second, the number of bits per character from 5 to 8, the stop bits, the parity, and whether the port works out the incoming speed by itself. The counters are read-only tallies of characters that arrived damaged, counted since the device last restarted.

sections.title: Control Signals
sections.content:
The input and output signal tables expose the hardware control signals. The signal name is one of eleven values, defined with reference to EIA Standard RS-232-C, August 1969: rts for Request to Send, cts for Clear to Send, dsr for Data Set Ready, dtr for Data Terminal Ready, ri for Ring Indicator, dcd for Received Line Signal Detector, sq for Signal Quality Detector, srs for Data Signaling Rate Selector, and srts, scts and sdcd for the secondary variants of Request to Send, Clear to Send and Received Line Signal Detector.

Each row gives the current signal state, with the values none, on and off, and a counter of the number of times the signal has changed from on to off or from off to on. Both tables use the same set of eleven names.

The synchronous port table also carries a set of SDLC-specific objects with default values. rs232SyncPortRole is dte or dce, defaulting to dce, naming the role the device is playing. rs232SyncPortEncoding is nrz or nrzi, defaulting to nrz, and names the bit stream encoding technique in effect. rs232SyncPortRTSControl is controlled or constant, defaulting to constant: in controlled mode a DTE asserts RTS each time data needs to be transmitted and drops RTS at some point after transmission begins, and a DCE issues CTS only after receiving RTS and waiting out the delay.

rs232SyncPortRTSCTSDelay is the interval in milliseconds that the DCE must wait after it sees RTS asserted before asserting CTS, defaulting to 0. The RFC says the object exists in support of older synchronous devices that cannot recognize CTS within a certain interval after asserting RTS. rs232SyncPortMode is fdx, hdx, simplex-receive or simplex-send, defaulting to fdx, and names the direction and simultaneity of data transfer. rs232SyncPortIdlePattern is mark or space, defaulting to space, and names the bit pattern used to indicate an idle line. rs232SyncPortMinFlags is the minimum number of flag patterns the port needs to recognize the end of one frame and the start of the next, with plausible values 1 and 2 and a default of 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The signal tables expose the control wires of the serial cable, such as Request to Send and Clear to Send. Each row gives the current state of the wire, as none, on or off, and a counter of how many times it has switched between on and off.

sections.title: Compliance and Security
sections.content:
The compliance statement makes the rs232Group mandatory for all SNMPv2 entities which have RS-232-like hardware interfaces. The rs232AsyncGroup is mandatory only for entities with asynchronous RS-232-like interfaces, and the rs232SyncGroup only for entities with synchronous RS-232-like interfaces. A separate rs232SyncSDLCGroup collects the SDLC-specific synchronous objects: the role, the encoding, the RTS control method, the RTS-to-CTS delay, the mode, the idle pattern and the minimum number of flags.

The Security Considerations section of the RFC says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Every device with a serial port must implement the general group of objects. The asynchronous group is only required on devices with asynchronous ports and the synchronous group only on devices with synchronous ports. The RFC says it does not discuss security.
